## Cause

`V3__drop_unused_indexes.sql` (commit 4d99828, "Q3 storage review") dropped `ux_payment_idempotency_key` — the unique index added by V2 specifically to close this race.

The review used zero reads in `pg_stat_user_indexes` as its "unused" signal. A unique index backing a constraint is never a lookup path, so it always reports zero reads; the count says nothing about whether it's load-bearing. V3's own comment records this.

The application-level check in `PaymentService.create` (`src/main/java/mn/payments/PaymentService.java:28`) is not a substitute. As V2's design note says, it's an optimisation — on a cluster, two concurrent requests with the same idempotency key can both see "no such payment" and both insert. The index was the thing that made the second insert fail.

## Fix

Added `src/main/resources/db/migration/V4__restore_payment_unique_index.sql`, recreating the index. I added a new migration rather than editing V3, since V3 has already been applied in production and Flyway would reject the checksum change.

I left `ix_payment_status_created` dropped — that one was a genuine lookup index with no evidence it's needed, and it isn't defined in any migration in this repo.

`mvn test` passes (no DB-backed tests exist to exercise this).

## Two things to check before you deploy

**The migration will fail if duplicates already exist.** Any rows written during the window when the index was absent will block `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`. Reconciling duplicate payment rows is a financial correction, so I deliberately didn't automate it in the migration — you'll want to identify and resolve those rows first:

```sql
SELECT idempotency_key, count(*) FROM payment GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1;
```

**`PaymentService.create` never sets the idempotency key on the row it saves** (`PaymentService.java:32-34`): the new `Payment` gets only `status`, and the entity exposes no setter for `idempotencyKey`, `amount`, or `id`. Taken literally, the persisted row can't carry the key, which would mean the index has nothing to enforce against and `existsByIdempotencyKey` could never match. This predates the double-charge regression — it's been that way since before V2 — so I suspect the file is abbreviated relative to what actually runs in production. Worth confirming against the deployed code; if it's real, the index fix alone won't hold, and I can follow up.

Separately, once the index is back, the losing side of a race gets a constraint violation propagated to the caller rather than the existing payment. That's the safe failure direction (rejected, not double-charged), but returning the existing payment would be better. It needs care — inside the current `@Transactional` method the transaction is already marked rollback-only when the violation fires, so the retry has to happen in a new transaction. Happy to do that as a separate change.
